source.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
source.authors: Anton Korznikov; Andrey V. Galichin; Alexey Dontsov; Oleg Y. Rogov; I. Oseledets; Elena Tutubalina

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests SAE feature recovery against synthetic ground truth and presents results that challenge whether SAE features or standard evaluation metrics establish meaningful feature decompositions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on synthetic feature recovery and real-activation SAE evaluations. Results cited from other work are not included. Real-activation proxy-metric results are recorded under none because they do not directly measure canonicality, completeness, or stability of SAE features.
record.test_reason: The synthetic experiment checks whether SAE dictionaries recover known ground-truth features, which bears on whether SAE features are complete units (V5). The real-activation frozen-baseline results argue that standard metrics cannot certify SAE latents as the model's features. Neither experiment trains a toy network or measures LLM neurons, so V1–V4 and V6 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that good reconstruction and standard SAE metrics do not certify meaningful feature decomposition. Three of four SAEs recover only 7–9% of synthetic features, and random frozen baselines match trained SAEs on proxy metrics. They frame this as a critique of evaluation methodology, not of SAEs as a paradigm.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates synthetic feature recovery and compares trained SAEs with random-component baselines; it does not reproduce the original toy-network setup or its measurements of superposition geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Synthetic feature recovery differed by architecture and activation-probability regime; variable-probability recovery favored high-frequency features. Real-activation results were reported across SAE architectures, layers, models, initialization schemes, and sparsity settings.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs whose decoder, encoder, or near-random decoder is frozen at random initialization match fully-trained SAEs on AutoInterp, sparse probing and RAVEL on Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3-8B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Standard SAE proxy metrics (interpretability, sparse probing, causal editing) do not distinguish learned dictionaries from random-direction baselines.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets
record.problems: Synthetic features are independently activated, a simplification the authors acknowledge; the synthetic experiment evaluates SAE recovery rather than learned feature geometry in a toy network. Ground truth is unavailable for the real LLM activations, so those results rely on proxy metrics. Main L0-sweep plots are single-seed; three-seed mean±standard deviation results are reported at L0=160. Some synthetic recovery results are reported only as ranges or qualitative descriptions.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed real-activation results for further architectures, models, layers, initialization schemes and metrics in Appendix D (Tables 3–5), and additional metrics in Appendix E, are not individually catalogued because they are proxy scores rather than direct measurements of canonical or complete feature recovery. Figure-only per-setting values not stated in text are also omitted.

untested.parts: Stability across seeds or runs, and canonicality of SAE features on real LLMs. Real-activation results are proxy metrics only.
No toy network is trained. Superposed data is generated directly, and no geometry or sparsity transition is measured.
Capacity competition and dedicated dimensions for important features are not tested.
Polysemantic neurons and their origins are not studied.
Whether LLM features are distributed or SAE-recoverable is not established, because ground truth is unknown on real activations.

missing.what: SynthSAEBench feature-recovery results (MMCS) for the four architectures at k=20 and k=100, under correlated features. Examples: TopK 0.644/0.825, BatchTopK 0.322/0.489.
Explained variance accompanying the synthetic recovery results: about 0.67 in the constant setting and 0.71 in the variable setting. This is needed to show the reconstruction–recovery disconnect.

record.verdict_notes: The synthetic data follows the superposition hypothesis but is generated directly (independent features, n=100, 3200 features), not learned by a toy network. It therefore bears on SAE recovery (V5), not on V1. Appendix B reports that TopK's synthetic advantage does not transfer to real activations by proxy metrics; the authors call it 'an artifact' of the setup. Real-activation results use single seeds in the sweeps, with 3 seeds at L0=160.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test toy networks' learned superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, or regular arrangements of overlapping directions.
Does not test neuron polysemanticity as competition for capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not measure naturally occurring polysemantic neurons or whether they arise without capacity pressure.
On real LLM activations, ground-truth features are unknown; the paper does not establish that LLM features are spread across neurons or that an SAE recovers actual sparse LLM features.
Tests recovery against known synthetic features and evaluates proxies on real activations, but does not test feature stability across runs or whether SAE features are canonical units of real LLMs.
Does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features or test the dimensionality of represented features.

relation.reason: The study directly measures recovery of known synthetic features, bearing on V5 rather than merely assuming or citing it.

tranche.reason: Known-feature recovery failures qualify V5's completeness claim; random-component controls demonstrate that standard proxy metrics cannot certify meaningful decomposition.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased. Synthetic recovery tests V5's completeness component; it does not establish stability, canonicity or exhaustive recovery in naturalistic LLM representations.
